title: Mohammedan Culture and Philosophy
orientation: This chapter surveys the rise of the Arab empire after Mahomet's death and the Islamic philosophical tradition that grew up within it, culminating in Avicenna and Averroes. It matters because Arabic philosophy preserved and transmitted Aristotle (heavily overlaid with Neoplatonism) to the medieval West at a time when Western Europe had largely lost direct access to Greek philosophy, and because Averroes's interpretation of Aristotle became a live issue within thirteenth-century Christian scholasticism.
historical_background: The Hegira of 622 marks the start of the Muslim era; Mahomet died in 632, and Arab conquests followed with extraordinary speed -- Syria, Persia, Egypt, and Spain were all overrun within a century, though the westward advance was checked at Tours in 732. Conquest was eased by the exhaustion of Persia and Byzantium, by persecuted religious minorities (Nestorians, Monophysites, Jews) welcoming a tolerant new ruler, and by the Arabs' relative lack of religious fanaticism. The Umayyad caliphate (to 750), based in Damascus, gave way to the Persian-backed Abbasids in Baghdad, whose early rulers (notably Harun-al-Rashid) presided over the caliphate's greatest splendour before it fractured into Umayyad Spain, Abbasid Persia/Iraq, and other independent regions, with the last Abbasid caliph killed by the Mongols in 1256.
philosophical_problems: The problem of universals: are genera and species anterior to things, in things, or only after things in the mind (Avicenna's synthesis of Platonic and Aristotelian views)?
Whether the existence of God can be proved by unaided reason, independent of revelation (Averroes)
Whether personal immortality survives if only the impersonal intellect (nous), and not the individual soul, is immortal (Averroes's reading of Aristotle's De Anima)

Whether philosophical/rational truth can conflict with revealed religious truth, and if so how the conflict should be resolved (Algazel vs. Averroes; Maimonides's reconciliation of Aristotle and Jewish theology)

philosophers_discussed.name: Kindi
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The first philosopher to write in Arabic (d. ca. 873) and the only philosopher of note who was himself an Arab; his translation of parts of Plotinus's Enneads under the title 'The Theology of Aristotle' caused lasting confusion between Aristotle and Neoplatonism in Arabic philosophy.

philosophers_discussed.name: Al-Khwarazmi
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Ninth-century Persian mathematician and astronomer who transmitted Sanskrit/Indian astronomical and numerical learning; his book, translated into Latin as 'Algoritmi de numero Indorum,' gave the West so-called 'Arabic' numerals, and his algebra text was used in the West until the sixteenth century.

philosophers_discussed.name: Omar Khayyam
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Described as the only man known to Russell who was both poet and mathematician; reformed the Persian calendar in 1079.

philosophers_discussed.name: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Persian philosopher and physician (980-1037), more famous among Mohammedans than Averroes; his philosophy is nearer to Aristotle and less Neoplatonic than his predecessors', and he developed an influential solution to the problem of universals ('before things, in things, and after things'); also hugely influential in medicine into the seventeenth century, though not a saintly character.

philosophers_discussed.name: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Spanish-Muslim philosopher and jurist (1126-1198), cadi of Cordova and Seville, physician to the Almohad rulers before being exiled on charges of heresy; sought to purify the Arabic Aristotle of Neoplatonic accretions, held that God's existence is provable by reason and that only the impersonal intellect (not the individual soul) is immortal; far more influential in Christian than in Mohammedan philosophy, where he was 'a dead end.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Algazel
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Orthodox theologian who wrote 'The Destruction of the Philosophers,' arguing that since all necessary truth is in the Koran there is no need for independent speculation; answered by Averroes's 'The Destruction of the Destruction.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Maimonides
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Spanish-Jewish philosopher (b. Cordova 1135, d. Cairo), author of 'Guide to Wanderers,' which sought to reconcile Aristotle with Jewish theology, holding that philosophy and revelation converge in the knowledge of God and that Scripture should be read allegorically where it conflicts with reason.

schools_discussed: Arabic/Mohammedan philosophy (Syrian, Persian, and Spanish branches)
Sufism (Persian Islamic mysticism, described by Russell as more or less Neoplatonic)
Nestorian Christianity (as a channel for Greek learning into the Muslim world)

core_concepts.name: Avicenna's threefold theory of universals
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Avicenna tries to reconcile Plato (universals exist before things) and Aristotle (universals exist in things) by saying universals exist in three ways: before things, as ideas in God's mind (God must have the idea 'cat' before creating cats); in things, as the common nature actually present in each particular (felinity in each created cat); and after things, in our minds, as the general idea we form by noticing resemblances among particulars we have observed.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that genera (universals) exist ante rem (in the divine understanding, prior to creation), in re (immanent in the created particulars themselves), and post rem (as abstracted concepts formed by the human mind after experience of particulars).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It offered a systematic reconciliation of the Platonic and Aristotelian positions on universals that later influenced Christian scholastic treatments of the same problem, including formulas echoed by Averroes and Albertus Magnus.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Formulated by Avicenna (980-1037) in the course of adjudicating between the conflicting views he found in Plato and in the two strands of Aristotle's own thought.
examples: God's idea of 'cat' prior to creating any cats (universals before things)
Felinity actually present in each created cat (universals in things)
The general idea 'cat' formed by a mind after observing many particular cats (universals after things)
competing_positions: Plato's view that universals are anterior to and independent of particular things
The Aristotelian view (when 'combating Plato') that universals exist only in and through particular things
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Avicenna's formula 'Thought brings about the generality in forms' was repeated by Averroes and Albertus Magnus, and the ante rem/in re/post rem framework recurs throughout later Christian scholastic discussions of universals, including in William of Occam.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Grounds the theory of universals explicitly in God's creative understanding, tying a logical/metaphysical doctrine to theology.

core_concepts.name: Averroes on reason, revelation, and the unity of intellect
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Averroes argued two things that got him into trouble with the pious: first, that reason alone (without revelation) can prove God exists; and second, following Aristotle, that while the individual soul is not immortal, 'intellect' (nous) is immortal -- but since intellect is one and the same in all people, this does not give any individual person personal survival after death.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The position that (a) God's existence is a truth demonstrable by unaided natural reason, and (b) what survives death is an impersonal, universal intellect rather than an individuated personal soul, since intellect is numerically one across all thinking beings.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It directly denied personal immortality, a doctrine central to popular religion, and so became the flashpoint for the 'Averroist' controversy that convulsed the University of Paris in the thirteenth century and that Thomas Aquinas set out to refute.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Averroes in his commentaries on Aristotle's De Anima, as his considered interpretation of Aristotle's own ambiguous remarks on nous.
examples: Russell's own judgment that the De Anima 'leads much more naturally to the view of Averroes than to that of Aquinas' (a claim made explicit in the next chapter but rooted in this one)
objections: Combated by Christian philosophers, above all Thomas Aquinas, precisely because it denies personal immortality
Regarded by orthodox Mohammedans as heretical, contributing to Averroes's own persecution and exile
competing_positions: Aquinas's view that each individual has his own immortal intellect, not a single intellect shared by all
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Produced 'Averroism' as an unprofessional free-thinking movement in medieval Europe, and shaped debate especially among Franciscans and at the University of Paris in the thirteenth century.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Averroes was exiled and his books burned by order of Caliph Al-Mansur after orthodox theologians accused him of preferring 'the philosophy of the ancients' to the true faith.

core_concepts.name: Islamic philosophy as transmission rather than original speculation
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell argues that Arabic philosophy, for all its historical importance, was not original: its logic and metaphysics came from Aristotle and the Neoplatonists, its medicine from Galen, its mathematics and astronomy from Greek and Indian sources, and its mystical religious thought had an admixture of old Persian belief. Its great historical service was to preserve and transmit ancient learning through the 'dark ages' that separated ancient from modern European civilization.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's thesis that Mohammedan (and, in a parallel way, Byzantine) civilization, while admirable in the arts and technical accomplishment, showed no real capacity for independent theoretical speculation, and functioned historically chiefly as a transmitter of ancient learning to the West, which then produced genuinely new thought (scholasticism from the Mohammedan stimulus, the Renaissance -- among other causes -- from the Byzantine one).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It frames how Russell wants readers to weigh Islamic philosophy's contribution: not for its own doctrines primarily, but for making the Aristotelian corpus and other ancient learning available to Western scholastics from the twelfth century onward.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell's own retrospective judgment, stated explicitly at the close of the chapter.
examples: Arabic writers showed real originality chiefly in mathematics and in chemistry (an incidental byproduct of alchemy)
Spanish Jews, who knew both Arabic and the Christians' language, served as translators bridging Moorish and Christian Spain
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Set up the transmission of Aristotle (via Latin translations, e.g. of Averroes by Michael Scott in the early thirteenth century) that made possible the scholastic synthesis covered in the following chapters.

arguments.title: Averroes's proof of God's existence by reason alone
premises: Reason, independent of revelation, is capable of establishing certain truths about the world
The existence of God is one such truth
arguments.conclusion: God's existence can be proved by reason without appeal to revelation.
arguments.explanation: Russell reports this as a position Averroes held in common with Thomas Aquinas, though Russell gives no detailed reconstruction of Averroes's specific proof in this chapter (Aquinas's fuller version of a similar argument, the unmoved mover, is treated in the chapter on Aquinas).
implications: If sound, it would mean philosophy and revealed religion converge on at least this one central theological truth without conflict

arguments.title: Averroes's 'double truth' defence against charges of unorthodoxy (as reported via Ueberweg)
premises: According to Muslim mystics, every text of the Koran has 7, 70, or 700 layers of interpretation
The literal meaning is intended only for the ignorant masses; the wise may understand a deeper, allegorical sense
Among so many possible interpretations there is likely to be at least one that agrees with what a given philosopher teaches
arguments.conclusion: A philosopher's teaching, understood allegorically, cannot straightforwardly be said to conflict with the Koran.
arguments.explanation: Russell reports this defence (offered on Averroes's behalf by the historian Ueberweg) with visible skepticism, noting dryly that whether Averroes was orthodox is 'a matter, one would say, for Muslims to decide,' and observing that the view that ordinary people should take the Koran literally while the wise need not was unlikely to win popular acceptance.
objections: Russell notes the ignorant populace objected to all learning beyond the Holy Book regardless of subtle allegorical defences
The elitist premise (truth for the wise, literalism for the vulgar) was politically untenable
implications: Illustrates the general strategy, later echoed in the Latin Averroist 'double truth' doctrine, of separating a philosophical truth (reason) from a theological truth (revelation) to avoid direct conflict

key_distinctions: Sunni vs. Shiah Islam (the latter followed Ali and regarded the Umayyads as usurpers; Persia was predominantly Shiah)
Universals ante rem, in re, and post rem (Avicenna's threefold distinction)
The soul (not immortal, per Averroes) vs. intellect/nous (impersonal and immortal)
Literal vs. allegorical interpretation of Scripture (the mystics' and Maimonides's distinction)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Arabic philosophy inherited its Aristotle already refracted through Neoplatonism (via Kindi's conflation of Plotinus with 'The Theology of Aristotle'), and via the Nestorians, who valued Aristotle chiefly for his logic, echoing the narrow late-antique reception of Aristotle described in earlier chapters on Boethius.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Averroes's Latin translation (by Michael Scott, early thirteenth century) made him a central and controversial authority for Christian scholastics, provoking 'Averroism' at the University of Paris and among Franciscans, and directly shaping the concerns Thomas Aquinas addresses in Summa contra Gentiles (treated in the following chapters).
political_social_context: The Arab empire was an absolute hereditary monarchy under the caliph; dynastic succession disputes, combined with polygamy, regularly produced succession wars. Philosophers depended on the patronage of relatively freethinking princes and were viewed with suspicion by a fanatical populace; Averroes's own exile shows how quickly royal favour toward philosophy could be withdrawn under religious pressure.
religion_science_culture_context: Arabic philosophers were characteristically encyclopedic, mixing what we would call philosophy with alchemy, astrology, astronomy, and zoology; commerce, agriculture (especially irrigation), and the maintenance of Roman/Persian road networks underpinned a civilization that Russell credits with real achievement in the arts and 'many technical ways' even while denying it independent theoretical originality.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Mohammedan civilization as historically important chiefly as a transmitter rather than an originator: it preserved and passed on Greek philosophy (heavily Neoplatonized), Indian mathematics and astronomy, and Galenic medicine, while itself producing, in his judgment, no philosopher of true originality apart from perhaps Kindi's role as first translator. He treats Avicenna and Averroes as essentially able commentators on Aristotle rather than independent thinkers, and frames Averroes's chief historical importance as lying in his effect on Christian rather than Mohammedan philosophy. Russell's tone toward Islamic philosophy is respectful of its historical function but consistently deflationary about its originality, a judgment he states explicitly and without much qualification.
critical_context: Common scholarly criticism: many historians of Islamic philosophy regard Russell's 'mere transmitters, not originators' framing as underestimating genuinely original contributions by figures such as Avicenna in metaphysics and philosophy of science, and Averroes's own systematic project of purifying Aristotle from Neoplatonic accretion (which Russell himself credits as a real achievement) sits uneasily with the blanket claim of non-originality.
key_takeaways: The rapid Arab conquests (632-732) succeeded partly through the exhaustion of Persia/Byzantium, the welcome of persecuted religious minorities, and Arab religious tolerance of 'the peoples of the Book.'
The Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates gave way, over time, to fragmentation into Spain, Persia, Egypt, and North Africa as separate power centers.
Avicenna offered an influential threefold ('before, in, after things') reconciliation of Platonic and Aristotelian views of universals.
Averroes held that God's existence is provable by reason and that only the impersonal intellect, not the individual soul, is immortal -- a view that provoked 'Averroism' in Christian Europe.
Maimonides, a Spanish Jew writing in Arabic, sought a parallel reconciliation of Aristotle with Jewish theology.
Russell judges Islamic philosophy historically vital as a transmitter of ancient learning to the West but lacking in independent theoretical originality.
study_notes:
This chapter functions as a bridge: it explains how Aristotle (mixed with a heavy dose of Neoplatonism) survived the early medieval period and re-entered Western Europe. Pay attention to the chain of transmission -- Syrian Nestorians to Arabic translators to Spanish Jewish and Christian translators -- because this same chain reappears in the following two chapters as the route by which the 'new' Aristotle reaches Paris and Oxford in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

The two philosophers Russell singles out, Avicenna and Averroes, illustrate two different relationships to power and orthodoxy: Avicenna moved fluidly between courts as a valued physician despite his unconventional personal life, while Averroes's philosophical standing collapsed rapidly once his patron withdrew support under pressure from religious conservatives. This pattern -- philosophy tolerated only at the pleasure of a friendly ruler, and vulnerable to sudden reversal -- recurs throughout the book's treatment of medieval thought, Christian as well as Muslim.

Finally, notice the seeds planted here for the thirteenth-century crisis over 'Averroism': the specific doctrine that intellect (not the individual soul) is immortal is what later gets Christian Averroists in trouble at Paris, and Thomas Aquinas's insistence on individual immortality (covered later) is written partly against the position first laid out by Averroes in this chapter.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Mahomet's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD, which marks the start of the Islamic calendar.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The emigration (hijra) of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, adopted as year one of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The political and religious successor to Mahomet who ruled the Islamic empire.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The head of the Islamic state as 'successor' (khalifa) to the Prophet, holding both political authority and inherited religious prestige; nominally elective but soon hereditary within the Umayyad and Abbasid dynasties.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A member of a mystical branch of Islam that sought direct, personal, often allegorical experience of religious truth.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: An adherent of Sufism, a mystical current within Islam, strong especially in Persia, that allowed itself wide latitude in mystical and allegorical interpretation of orthodox dogma; Russell describes it as 'more or less Neoplatonic.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The Greek philosophical term for 'intellect' or the rational, thinking part of the mind, as distinct from the individual soul.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Aristotelian psychology, the faculty of intellectual understanding; Averroes held nous to be one and impersonal across all thinkers, and therefore immortal, in contrast to the individual, non-immortal soul.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A movement of thinkers, mostly outside the clergy, who followed Averroes's teaching that only an impersonal intellect (not the individual soul) survives death, thereby denying personal immortality.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The philosophical current, influential especially among Franciscans and at the University of Paris in the thirteenth century, that adopted Averroes's interpretation of Aristotle on the unity and impersonality of the active intellect, provoking ecclesiastical condemnation.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what circumstances helped the early Arab conquests succeed so rapidly?
questions.answer: The exhaustion of Persia and the Eastern Empire from long wars; persecuted religious groups (Nestorian Syrians, Monophysite Egyptians, Jews in Spain) welcoming Muslim rule as preferable to Catholic or Visigothic persecution; and the comparative lack of religious fanaticism among the conquering Arabs, whose motive was largely plunder and wealth, which allowed a small ruling minority to govern vast, more sophisticated populations without much friction.
questions.explanation: Russell stresses that toleration and lightened taxation, more than military overmatch, explain the speed and durability of the conquests.

questions.prompt: Which Mohammedan philosopher argued that universals exist 'before things, in things, and after things,' reconciling Plato's and Aristotle's views?
questions.explanation: This threefold formula -- universals in God's understanding before creation, in created things themselves, and in the human mind after abstraction from experience -- is Avicenna's distinctive contribution to the medieval debate on universals.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher held that the individual soul is not immortal but that intellect (nous), being impersonal and the same in all people, is immortal?
questions.explanation: This doctrine denied personal immortality and later fueled the 'Averroist' controversy among Christian scholastics.

questions.prompt: Compare Avicenna's and Averroes's relationships with political power and religious authority.
questions.answer: Avicenna moved between courts across Persia, protected by rulers who valued his medical skill despite his unorthodox personal conduct (a taste for wine and women) and the suspicion of theologians; he was never formally condemned or exiled. Averroes, by contrast, enjoyed similar royal patronage in Cordova and Seville but was ultimately deprived of his position and exiled by Caliph Al-Mansur under pressure from orthodox opposition, and books on logic and metaphysics were publicly burned, though he may have been restored to favour shortly before death.
questions.explanation: The contrast illustrates how precarious philosophical patronage could be even for the most eminent thinkers when religious conservatives turned political opinion against them.

questions.prompt: What was Algazel's argument against philosophy in 'The Destruction of the Philosophers,' and how did Averroes respond?
questions.answer: Algazel argued that since all necessary truth is already contained in the Koran, there is no need for speculation independent of revelation, upholding in particular the creation of the world in time out of nothing, the reality of the divine attributes, and bodily resurrection. Averroes responded with a book titled 'The Destruction of the Destruction,' treating religion as containing philosophic truth in allegorical form -- for instance interpreting creation in an Aristotelian fashion.
questions.explanation: This exchange exemplifies the broader tension in the chapter between orthodox theology and philosophical rationalism within Islam.

questions.prompt: What role did the Jews of Spain play in transmitting Mohammedan philosophy to Christian Europe?
questions.answer: Knowing both Arabic (from living under Moorish rule) and the language of the Christian conquerors, Spanish Jews were able to supply translations bridging the two worlds, especially after Christian reconquest; Jewish communities in Provence also sheltered Moorish philosophers fleeing persecution of Aristotelians in the thirteenth century.
questions.explanation: This transmission role is exemplified by Maimonides, whose 'Guide to Wanderers' was translated from Arabic into Hebrew and then into Latin.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Ueberweg's defence of Averroes against charges of unorthodoxy, and explain why Russell treats it skeptically.
questions.answer: The defence runs: mystics held every Koranic text has up to 700 layers of interpretation, with the literal sense reserved for the ignorant; therefore among so many possible interpretations there should be one matching any given philosophical claim, so a philosopher's teaching cannot really conflict with the Koran. Russell is skeptical because whether Averroes was orthodox is really a question for Muslims themselves to judge, and because the elitist premise -- that ordinary people take Scripture literally while the wise may not -- was unlikely to win broad popular acceptance, which is exactly what happened: the populace remained hostile to speculative learning.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this passage partly to illustrate the general strategy of reconciling philosophy and revealed religion through allegorical reading, a strategy also used by Maimonides.

flashcards.front: What was the Hegira and when did it occur?
flashcards.back: Mahomet's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD, marking the start of the Islamic calendar.

flashcards.front: What battle in 732 halted the westward advance of Muslim conquest into Europe?
Name the two main Islamic dynasties covered in this chapter and their capitals.
flashcards.back: The Umayyads (capital Damascus, to 750) and the Abbasids (capital Baghdad, from 750).

flashcards.front: Who was the first person to write philosophy in Arabic, and what confusion did he introduce?
flashcards.back: Kindi (d. ca. 873); his translation of Plotinus's Enneads under the title 'The Theology of Aristotle' conflated Neoplatonism with genuine Aristotle.

flashcards.front: Who transmitted 'Arabic' numerals (actually Indian in origin) to the West, and in what work?
flashcards.back: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarazmi, in a book translated into Latin as 'Algoritmi de numero Indorum.'

flashcards.front: What are Avicenna's dates and where was he active?
flashcards.back: 980-1037; active across Persia (Bokhara, Khiva, Khorassan, Ispahan, Teheran).

flashcards.front: State Avicenna's threefold account of universals.
flashcards.back: Universals exist before things (in God's understanding), in things (as natures immanent in particulars), and after things (as concepts abstracted by the human mind).

flashcards.front: What are Averroes's dates and where was he from?
What was Averroes's position on the immortality of the soul?
flashcards.back: The individual soul is not immortal, but intellect (nous) is -- though since intellect is one and impersonal across all thinkers, this does not secure personal immortality.

flashcards.front: What book did Algazel write against philosophy, and how did Averroes respond?
flashcards.back: 'Destruction of the Philosophers'; Averroes replied with 'Destruction of the Destruction.'

flashcards.front: Who was Maimonides and what was his major work?
flashcards.back: A Spanish-Jewish philosopher (b. Cordova, 1135) who wrote 'Guide to Wanderers,' reconciling Aristotle with Jewish theology.

flashcards.front: According to Russell, what was the main historical importance of Mohammedan civilization for Western philosophy?
flashcards.back: As a transmitter of ancient (Greek, Persian, and Indian) learning to the West during the 'dark ages,' rather than as a source of original speculation.

quiz.prompt: In what year did the Hegira, marking the start of the Muslim era, take place?
quiz.explanation: The Hegira, Mahomet's flight from Mecca to Medina, occurred in 622 AD.

quiz.prompt: Which battle in 732 halted the further westward expansion of the Mohammedans into Europe?
quiz.explanation: The Mohammedans were defeated at the Battle of Tours in 732, exactly one hundred years after Mahomet's death.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, Avicenna was primarily famous in the West for his philosophy rather than his medicine.
quiz.explanation: Russell says Avicenna was even more famous in medicine than philosophy, and was used in Europe as a guide to medicine from the twelfth to the seventeenth century.

quiz.prompt: According to Avicenna, where do universals exist 'before things'?
options: Nowhere -- they do not exist before things
quiz.explanation: Avicenna holds that universals exist before things as ideas in God's understanding -- for example, God's idea 'cat' precedes the creation of particular cats.

quiz.prompt: What happened to Averroes after Caliph Al-Mansur turned against him under pressure from the orthodox?
options: He was deprived of his position and exiled, and his books on logic and metaphysics were burned
He was made chief judge of Cordova
quiz.explanation: Al-Mansur exiled Averroes, first near Cordova and then to Morocco, and ordered the burning of his books on logic and metaphysics, though he may have been restored to favour shortly before his death.
quiz.related_concept: Averroes on reason, revelation, and the unity of intellect

quiz.prompt: What was distinctive about Averroes's view of the immortality of intellect (nous)?
options: That neither soul nor intellect survives death
That intellect is immortal but is one and impersonal, shared across all thinkers, so personal immortality is not secured
That each person's intellect is individually immortal
That intellect is immortal only for prophets
quiz.explanation: Averroes held, following his reading of Aristotle, that the soul is not immortal but intellect is -- yet since intellect is one and the same across different persons, this does not secure personal immortality, a view later combated by Christian philosophers.
quiz.related_concept: Averroes on reason, revelation, and the unity of intellect

quiz.prompt: Algazel's book 'Destruction of the Philosophers' was answered by Averroes's book titled 'Destruction of the ____.'
quiz.explanation: Averroes titled his reply 'Destruction of the Destruction.'
quiz.related_concept: Averroes on reason, revelation, and the unity of intellect

quiz.prompt: What was the title and purpose of Maimonides's major philosophical work?
options: 'Guide to Wanderers,' reconciling Aristotle with Jewish theology
'Destruction of the Philosophers,' refuting Greek philosophy
quiz.explanation: Maimonides wrote 'Guide to Wanderers,' addressed to philosophers who had lost their faith, aiming to reconcile Aristotle (authoritative on the sublunary world) with Jewish revelation (authoritative on the heavenly).
quiz.related_concept: Islamic philosophy as transmission rather than original speculation

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, in which two fields did Arabic writers show genuine originality?
quiz.explanation: Russell credits Arabic writers with originality chiefly in mathematics and in chemistry, the latter an incidental result of alchemical research.
quiz.related_concept: Islamic philosophy as transmission rather than original speculation

essay_prompts.prompt: Explain Russell's claim that Mohammedan civilization's chief importance for Western philosophy lay in transmission rather than original speculation. Do the cases of Avicenna and Averroes support or complicate this claim?
rubric: Uses specific evidence from the chapter (Kindi, al-Khwarazmi, Avicenna, Averroes)
Considers counter-evidence, such as Avicenna's and Averroes's genuine synthetic/interpretive achievements

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Averroes's view that only impersonal intellect is immortal with the concerns this later raised for Christian Averroists at the University of Paris, as anticipated in this chapter.
rubric: States Averroes's position on soul vs. intellect accurately
Explains why the doctrine denies personal immortality
Connects the doctrine's later reception among Christian Averroists
Engages with why this provoked theological controversy
